name: MeatLink B2B Meat Commerce Platform
description: Live B2B meat sourcing and commerce platform for Indonesian food businesses, with role-based data security, Midtrans payments, and an OAuth-protected MCP server that AI agents can use safely.

screenshots.alt: MeatLink homepage for business meat procurement

problem: Restaurants, hotels, caterers, and butcher shops in Indonesia often buy meat through scattered WhatsApp chats and supplier price lists, with little visibility into stock, grades, or fair per-kilogram prices. Suppliers lack a simple channel to reach business buyers, and beef-market intelligence is spread across FAOSTAT, USDA, and Indonesian government sources.
solution: Built meatlink.id with a partner as a full B2B commerce platform: catalog and search with transparent per-kilogram pricing, multi-item RFQs with reference tracking, cart and checkout with Midtrans payments, orders and invoices, and admin and vendor consoles for inventory, AI-assisted spreadsheet import, payment reconciliation, and reporting. It runs TanStack Start on Cloudflare Workers with Supabase Postgres and exposes an OAuth 2.1-protected MCP server, so AI agents can check stock, place and look up orders, and draft market insights. A separate analytical engine runs a Codex research agent that turns public market data into bilingual EN/ID insight drafts without ever holding database credentials.
proof: Row-Level Security policies per role (anonymous, buyer organization, vendor organization, platform admin), checked against a written RLS test matrix after every policy change.

Hardened payment lifecycle: Midtrans webhook handling, 24-hour payment expiry aligned with order cancellation, a scheduled sync every 30 minutes, and an admin-only daily reconciliation that flags mismatches instead of force-settling orders.

MCP endpoint at meatlink.id/mcp with tools for stock, orders, market data, and insight drafts; server-side gates enforce evidence freshness, block internal marketplace data, and require complete English and Indonesian text.
AI writes are draft-only: every agent-generated insight is reviewed, edited, and published by a human from the admin console.
Built with an AI-native workflow (Lovable, Codex) while owning the architecture, data model, security policies, integrations, Vitest test suites, k6 load-test scenarios, and operational runbook.
result: MeatLink is live at meatlink.id with a self-serve catalog, RFQ, and checkout flow plus WhatsApp handoff for sales follow-up. It also demonstrates an agent-ready architecture: AI agents get authenticated, useful access to the business through MCP, while data privacy, evidence quality, and publishing stay under explicit server-side and human control.

architecture.alt: MeatLink system architecture: buyers, vendors, operations and AI agents reach one TanStack Start app on Cloudflare Workers, backed by Supabase with Row-Level Security, Midtrans, scheduled jobs and an AI insight pipeline behind the MCP boundary
architecture.caption: One TanStack Start app on Cloudflare Workers serves buyers, vendors and operations. Supabase Row-Level Security guards every role, and AI agents reach the business only through the OAuth-protected MCP endpoint, where server-side gates and human review decide what gets published.

name: DNDMind AI Copilot
description: Full-stack AI Dungeon Master copilot with RAG, memory retrieval, structured outputs, tool calling, and deterministic evaluation workflows.

screenshots.alt: DNDMind command center character workspace
DNDMind command center encounter workspace

problem: Tabletop role-playing sessions create a lot of changing context: character state, campaign memory, rules references, prior decisions, and narrative continuity. A simple chatbot can respond creatively, but it does not reliably preserve memory, retrieve relevant context, or keep outputs structured enough for repeatable gameplay support.
solution: Built a full-stack AI Dungeon Master copilot using Gemini 2.5 Flash for generation, plus application workflow, backend APIs, retrieval, memory, and structured AI responses. The system uses a Next.js interface, ASP.NET Core services, FastAPI inference support, PostgreSQL with pgvector, Docker Compose, embeddings, memory retrieval, tool/function calling, and deterministic evaluation workflows.
proof: Implements RAG and vector retrieval through PostgreSQL + pgvector instead of relying only on prompt history.
Separates frontend, backend, inference, and database responsibilities across a multi-service Docker Compose setup.
Uses Gemini 2.5 Flash with structured AI outputs and tool/function calling patterns to make responses easier to validate and integrate.
result: The project demonstrates production-style AI application architecture beyond a prompt-only demo: persistent memory, retrieval, structured outputs, backend orchestration, and evaluation-ready workflows.

architecture.alt: DNDMind architecture: Next.js client, ASP.NET Core API, Python FastAPI AI worker with Gemini, PostgreSQL with pgvector indices, guardrails and an evaluation suite, deployed on Cloud Run
architecture.caption: The Next.js client talks to an ASP.NET Core API that owns campaign data in PostgreSQL. A Python FastAPI worker handles generation, retrieval over separate rules and homebrew indices in pgvector, tool calls and guardrail checks, and a deterministic evaluation suite runs against the same pipeline.

name: RASCI STK Process Governance & Document Generator
description: Internal platform, branded PRISMA, that turns RASCI process hierarchies into controlled STK documents, with revisioned content, DOCX and PDF generation from corporate templates, and an AI module that drafts sections and draws cross-functional flow diagrams.

screenshots.alt: PRISMA dashboard with STK status counts, the RASCI gap and overlap chart and the role distribution donut
STK generator on the content step, with the sticky document header and revision selector
The AI drafting dialog asking what the document should cover before it drafts every section
Business process map with level and RASCI role filters, process counts and the hierarchy list

problem: Nusantara Regas documents its business processes as RASCI matrices and a hierarchy of STK documents: Pedoman, TKO, TKI and TKPA. The matrices lived in spreadsheets, the documents were written by hand in Word from a controlled template, and nobody could see at a glance which process still lacked a document, which roles overlapped, or which revision was current. Writing the first draft of a procedure was the slowest step of all.
solution: I led the team that built RASCI STK, a hosted Blazor WebAssembly application on .NET 8, and took three parts of it hands-on. I reworked the UI/UX: design tokens, shared grid components, a stepper-based STK generator with a sticky document header, and an inbox where a row click runs the document's next action. I owned the reliability work: JWT validation with key rotation and clean expiry handling, revision-scoped content and attachments, nvarchar migrations so non-Latin text survives, and test layers from xUnit and bUnit to database procedure checks and a Playwright browser run. And I built the AI module end to end: an LLM client against an OpenAI-compatible gateway, a service that drafts every section of a document as a placeholder template, writes a single section using the rest of the revision as context, and generates cross-functional flow diagrams as validated JSON rendered to SVG and attached as images.
proof: Hosted Blazor WebAssembly on .NET 8: a WASM client, an ASP.NET Core API that hosts it, shared DTOs, EF Core for entity CRUD, and Dapper with stored procedures for the RASCI hierarchy, pivots and dashboards.

Document generation merges revision-scoped content, custom sub-sections and attachments into the corporate Word templates with Syncfusion DocIO and converts to PDF; tests inspect the output for header values, section openings and leftover placeholders.

AI features stay inside the server layer: the client never talks to the model. The server loads the document context, forbids inventing facts the context lacks, sanitises replies to an allowed XHTML subset, retries a malformed reply once, and only replaces editor text until the author saves.

Flow diagrams are produced as structured JSON (roles, steps, boxes, arrows), validated, drawn by a deterministic SVG renderer and exported to JPG, so the diagram template is changed in the renderer rather than in the prompt.

Authentication tries the corporate endpoint first and falls back to local accounts hashed with ASP.NET Identity; every API action validates the token inline, and permission rows gate both sidebar entries and per-page buttons.

Reliability improvements I owned: expired tokens answer 401 and return to login, historical-key fallback for JWT rotation, idempotent add-on migration scripts for production, and conversion of legacy text columns to nvarchar(max).
result: Process owners now browse the RASCI hierarchy, run gap and overlap analysis, and start a controlled document from the process node itself. Authors get a first draft in minutes instead of a blank template, and every generated Pedoman, TKO, TKI and TKPA leaves the system as a template-faithful PDF with its revision history intact.

architecture.alt: RASCI STK architecture: a Blazor WebAssembly client on an ASP.NET Core API with EF Core and Dapper on SQL Server, Syncfusion DocIO for documents, an AI module calling an OpenAI-compatible gateway from the server, and a band of reliability work covering tokens, text integrity, document fidelity and test layers
architecture.caption: A hosted Blazor WebAssembly client on an ASP.NET Core API, EF Core and Dapper on SQL Server, DocIO for document generation, and an AI module that talks to an OpenAI-compatible gateway from the server only. The highlighted parts, the client UI/UX, the AI module and the reliability work, are the ones I built myself while leading the team.

name: Enterprise RAG Knowledge Assistant
description: On-premise LLM assistant redesigned into a retrieval pipeline with document chunking, embeddings, vector retrieval, contextual prompts, and output handling.

screenshots.alt: Enterprise RAG assistant showing retrieved IT security policy document
Enterprise RAG assistant welcome screen

problem: Internal operational knowledge was spread across documents, systems, and teams. A generic assistant could answer questions, but without retrieval grounding it risked incomplete context, inconsistent answers, and hallucination in an enterprise environment where reliability matters.
solution: Architected an on-premise Qwen-powered internal knowledge assistant and redesigned it into a RAG pipeline. The system uses document chunking, embedding generation, vector retrieval, contextual prompt orchestration, backend inference services, and enterprise UI integration.
proof: Designed the assistant for an on-premise enterprise environment rather than a public-only API workflow.
Moved from simple prompting toward retrieval-grounded answers using chunking, embeddings, vector retrieval, and context assembly.
Used Qwen with controlled response/output handling to reduce hallucination risk and make answers easier to integrate into internal workflows.
result: Improved the architecture of an internal AI assistant from general chat behavior into a more reliable enterprise knowledge workflow with retrieval grounding and clearer backend integration boundaries.

architecture.alt: Enterprise RAG architecture: documents are chunked and embedded into a vector index; at question time the backend retrieves passages, assembles a grounded prompt for an on-premise Qwen model and checks the output before the enterprise UI shows it
architecture.caption: Documents and SOPs are chunked and embedded into a vector index ahead of time. At question time the backend retrieves the most relevant passages, assembles a grounded prompt for the on-premise Qwen model, and checks the answer before it reaches the enterprise UI. Nothing leaves the company network.

name: Portfolio Assistant: Retrieval-Augmented Chat on a Static Site
description: The "Ask about my work" panel on this site: a retrieval-augmented assistant that answers recruiters' questions from the published case studies and resume, streams answers from Groq through the site's only server route, and ships with retrieval tests and a 33-question eval.

screenshots.alt: The assistant panel open on a case-study page, answering which projects used .NET with linked case studies
An answer about the permit-to-work platform with the source line linking the case study it was drawn from
The assistant panel on a phone-sized screen with the suggested questions

problem: Recruiters land on a portfolio with eighteen other case studies and a two-page resume and have about ninety seconds. They want answers to specific questions: has he shipped .NET 10, has he led teams, is he open to remote work. A search box cannot answer those, and a generic chatbot that invents a job title would be worse than nothing. The site is fully static on a free hosting tier, and the only free LLM access, Groq's free tier, allows about 8,000 tokens a minute, so a chatbot that stuffs the whole profile into every prompt would fail on its first question.
solution: I built the assistant as a small retrieval-augmented system inside the site. At load, the API route builds a BM25 index over chunks cut from the same JSON that renders the pages: each case study's overview, solution and proof, the experience timeline, the About strengths, and a facts file for the few things that live nowhere else, such as title, languages and availability. Each question retrieves the top three chunks, adds the profile facts and a one-line-per-case-study directory, and sends about 2,000 tokens to Groq with a system prompt that allows answers only from that context, requires a plain admission when the context is missing, links the relevant case study, and declines off-topic requests. The answer streams back as text with the cited sources in a header; the widget renders a safe subset of markdown and keeps the conversation in session storage across page navigations. Everything else on the site stays prerendered: this is the only server route.
proof: Grounded by construction: the corpus is generated from projects.json, experiences.json, about.json and assistant.json at module load, so the assistant cannot drift from the published pages.

Sized for the free tier: BM25 selects three chunks under a 4,500-character budget, so a question costs about 2,000 tokens against Groq's 8,000-tokens-per-minute limit, with a fallback model when the primary is rate-limited.

Guardrails on the server: message count and size caps, a per-instance per-IP limit, a 30-second upstream timeout, optional Cloudflare Turnstile, and a system prompt that refuses to invent facts or follow instructions embedded in questions.
Honest citations: the source line appears only when retrieval is confident, a clear top score with hits at least half as strong, so a weak match is never dressed up as evidence.

Tested at two levels: node --test retrieval checks that every case study is indexed and that recruiter questions rank the right one first, and a 33-question eval with required and forbidden phrases, covering co-founder framing, phone-number refusal, prompt injection and an Indonesian question, run against the live endpoint.
Zero added weight on the pages: one Astro component and a few hundred lines of script; no model runs in the browser and no key reaches it.
result: Visitors get specific, cited answers in a couple of seconds, and the assistant admits what the site does not say instead of guessing. The eval passes 33 of 33 questions against the live endpoint at the time of writing. It costs nothing to run at portfolio traffic, and it doubles as a live demonstration of the retrieval, prompt and evaluation discipline described in the other AI case studies.

architecture.alt: Portfolio assistant architecture: visitors use the widget on the static Astro site, which posts to the single server route; the route validates and rate-limits, retrieves BM25 chunks from the site's own JSON, builds a 2,000-token context and streams the answer from Groq, returning source links; evidence band with retrieval tests, the 33-question eval, confidence-gated citations and nothing running in the browser
architecture.caption: The widget posts to the one server route on an otherwise static site. The route validates and limits the request, retrieves three chunks from a BM25 index built over the same JSON that renders the pages, adds the profile facts and case-study directory, and streams Groq's answer back with its sources. The green band is what makes it trustworthy: retrieval tests, a 33-question eval and citations that only appear when retrieval is confident.

name: NR PTW Online Permit-to-Work Platform
description: Digital permit-to-work lifecycle for an LNG regasification operator: drafts, HSE validation, area-owner approval, issuance, suspension, renewal and closure, with every transition an explicit idempotent command and an official print package rendered from an immutable snapshot.

screenshots.alt: Papan Operasi monitoring board with issued, suspended and expiring permit metrics and the permit list under supervision
A requester's PTW Saya list with official permit numbers, status badges, search and page size
Buat draft PTW form filled by the demo auto-fill, with location, contractor, permit class and header classification
Draft preview of the official FM-001 hot work form rendered by the worker, carrying the DRAFT / TIDAK BERLAKU watermark

problem: Permits to work at Nusantara Regas were paper forms: FM-001, FM-002 and FM-003 for hot work, cold work and confined-space entry. Every approval chain ran on hardcopy, permit numbers were assigned by hand, nobody could see which permits were live across the terminal, and a form that failed HSE validation went back and forth without a record. Field control still had to stay on the signed paper for compliance, so a pure digital replacement was not an option.
solution: I designed and built NR PTW Online as a hybrid digital-to-paper system: a modular monolith on .NET 10 with an Angular 22 front end. The system owns the lifecycle from a requester's draft through sponsor approval, HSE validation, area-owner review of operating conditions, approval and issuance, suspension and resumption, renewal into a successor permit, and closure with digital verification. Every transition is a named command carrying an If-Match ETag and an Idempotency-Key; the aggregate, its task or decision, the audit event, the outbox message and the idempotency result commit in one transaction. A background worker renders the official print package from an immutable snapshot onto the controlled form as a vector template, with retry and backoff when rendering fails, and only READY packages count as official documents.
proof: Domain state machine with eleven states and a PermitVersion rule under which only a resubmission after REVISION_REQUIRED raises the business version; concurrency is handled by ETags on every aggregate.

Separation of duty enforced server-side: a sponsor who is also PIC HSE may validate their own permit, but Section 7 review and issuance always need a different role, and delegated managers are recorded and printed as PJS.
Official permit numbers in the PTW/NNNN/DD/MM/YYYY format are allocated inside the submit transaction from a per-year sequence table, so concurrent submits produce no gaps or duplicates.
Attachments are checked for PDF, JPEG and PNG signatures, hashed with SHA-256, tied to an exact version and print package, and carry malware-scan evidence; anything not CLEAN cannot be downloaded.
Login verifies credentials against Active Directory through the corporate Portal API with a local password fallback, HTTP-only cookie sessions, per-address rate limiting and account lockout.

Quality gates: xUnit domain tests, integration tests through the API factory on a disposable SQL Server in Testcontainers, print-layout regression tests, Vitest on the SPA, and decision records for the workflow baseline and all 18 UAT findings.
result: Users and stakeholders signed off the operational baseline on 25 September 2026, the UAT of 12 October 2026 closed its 18 findings within the following fortnight, and the user guide is generated from the running system with Playwright screenshots. Area owners now see every live, suspended and expiring permit on one board, while the signed hardcopy remains the field document.

architecture.alt: NR PTW Online architecture: requester, sponsor, HSE and area-owner users reach an Angular SPA behind nginx, a thin ASP.NET Core API over Application and Domain layers, EF Core with a transactional outbox, a worker that renders print packages, SQL Server, attachment volumes, the Portal API for Active Directory login, and the official print package
architecture.caption: An Angular SPA behind nginx talks to a thin ASP.NET Core API. Use cases, authorization and location scope live in the Application layer, the state machine in the Domain, and EF Core with a transactional outbox in Infrastructure. A separate worker drains the outbox and renders print packages from immutable snapshots, and SQL Server allocates the yearly permit number inside the same transaction as the submit.

name: NR EMAS Risk Monitoring
description: Enterprise risk evaluation and monitoring platform replacing Excel-based tracking with risk registers, treatment plans, KRI monitoring, approvals, and executive dashboards.

screenshots.alt: NR EMAS dashboard showing risk exposure and risk treatment monitoring
NR EMAS traffic light monitoring table and issues next steps panel

problem: Enterprise risk tracking was fragmented across Excel files and manual reporting flows. Risk registers, treatment plans, KRI monitoring, action plans, approvals, and dashboard reporting needed a centralized system so risk owners and executives could work from the same operational source.
solution: Led the development of NR EMAS, directing the developer who built it as a .NET platform with Clean Architecture: a Blazor (MudBlazor) interface, Web API, EF Core on SQL Server, MediatR, Hangfire background jobs, Serilog and Application Insights logging, and xUnit tests. The platform centralizes risk registers and treatment plans, routes action plans through a Manager, VP, and Risk Management approval chain, tracks KRIs and treatment progress, and gives executives real-time dashboards. Personally handled the production rollout: Docker deployment, an Nginx SSL reverse proxy, SQL Server initialization, and email notifications through the company Portal API.
proof: Public Rewire success story describes NR EMAS as replacing Excel-based risk tracking with a centralized workflow-driven platform.

Clean Architecture separates risk domain rules, application workflows (MediatR), infrastructure (EF Core, Hangfire), and the Blazor presentation layer, keeping the risk logic maintainable and testable with xUnit.
Risk workflows cover register import, top-risk weighting, periodic monitoring, multi-level approvals, and a full audit trail.
Production rollout owned end to end: containerized deployment, Nginx SSL reverse proxy, SQL Server initialization scripts, and Portal API email integration.
result: Moved risk monitoring from spreadsheet-based tracking into a centralized production platform with clearer ownership, structured approvals, KRI visibility, and real-time executive risk dashboards.

architecture.alt: NR EMAS architecture: Blazor UI and Web API on .NET Clean Architecture with MediatR, EF Core on SQL Server and Hangfire jobs, deployed in Docker behind an Nginx SSL reverse proxy with Portal API email
architecture.caption: A .NET Clean Architecture platform: a Blazor UI on a Web API, MediatR application workflows, EF Core on SQL Server and Hangfire background jobs. I directed the build and owned the production rollout: Docker, an Nginx SSL reverse proxy, SQL Server initialisation and Portal API email.

name: NR-CSR Program, Approval & Payment Management
description: Corporate social responsibility management system: proposal intake, eligibility, multi-level evaluation and survey approvals, budgets and work programs, payment requests exported to the group payment platform, vendor and legal documents, and reporting. Modernised from Laravel 6 on Oracle to Laravel 8 on PostgreSQL 16.

screenshots.alt: NR-CSR budget monitoring dashboard with annual budget, realisation and remaining budget, split by SDG pillar and priority
Realisation list recording donations and contract instalments with reference numbers, recipients, amounts and evidence
Work program planning page with the annual budget, allocated program budget and remaining budget
Monitoring and evaluation page listing program documents, evaluations and periodic reports per work program

problem: CSR at Nusantara Regas runs through a long chain: a proposal is checked for eligibility, evaluated, surveyed and approved level by level up to the CEO, then funded from annual budgets and work programs, paid in instalments through the group's POPAY payment platform, and reported per pillar and SDG. The existing application carried that chain on Laravel 6 against an Oracle database that was being retired, with no static analysis, no CI, and production on an offline IIS server where every deployment was manual and risky.
solution: I own NR-CSR end to end. I upgraded the framework from Laravel 6 to 8, migrated the schema and every environment from Oracle to PostgreSQL 16 and removed the Oracle driver, and restructured the code into Form Requests, Actions and Services behind domain route files with role middleware. I kept the Indonesian domain model and its 68 Eloquent and read-only view models intact, hardened authentication with LDAP fallback and email OTP, added liveness and dependency health endpoints for monitoring, and built the in-app user manual from screenshots of a test-seeded instance. The quality bar now runs in CI: a hardcoded-secret guardrail, PHPStan level 5, PHP-CS-Fixer and P0 to P2 regression suites on PHP 7.4 and 8.1.
proof: Laravel 6 to 8 upgrade and Oracle to PostgreSQL migration delivered in October 2026 as the first steps of a written dependency-hygiene plan, with the schema conversion tooling kept in the repository.

Layered request pipeline: domain route files, login and inactivity-timeout middleware, narrow role aliases such as isAdmin, isApprove, isFinance, isLegal and isSubsidiary, 83 Form Request classes and single-purpose Actions and Services.

POPAY integration through a Guzzle wrapper: payment requests are created and listed per approved proposal and the platform calls back a status endpoint; JSON responses share one envelope with centralised exception mapping.
Reporting through 34 Excel export classes, DataTables grids and printable views, plus dashboards by pillar, priority and program for budget monitoring.
Two deployment shapes from one codebase: nginx, PHP-FPM and PostgreSQL in Docker for development and CI, and an offline IIS child application with PHP FastCGI for production.
Guardrails on every push: secret scan, PHPStan with Larastan, PHP-CS-Fixer and the critical regression suites, with a PHP 8.1 validation runner alongside the 7.4 baseline.
result: The platform now runs on a supported framework and a single database engine across local, container and production environments, with every deployment reproducible from the repository. Finance exports payment requests straight to POPAY instead of re-keying them, and the October 2026 releases simplified realisation per instalment so donations and contract payments are recorded once, with their evidence, and flow into the recap reports without re-entry.

architecture.alt: NR-CSR architecture: inputers, approvers, finance, legal and subsidiary users reach a Laravel 8 application on PHP 7.4 behind IIS or nginx, structured as routes and middleware, authentication with LDAP fallback and OTP, controllers with Form Requests, Actions and Services, Eloquent models and reporting, on PostgreSQL 16 with POPAY, LDAP, SMTP and monitoring integrations, plus a band of modernisation work
architecture.caption: Users reach the Laravel 8 application through IIS in production or nginx in Docker. Requests flow from domain route files and role middleware through Form Requests, Actions and Services to Eloquent models on PostgreSQL 16. POPAY, LDAP, SMTP and a monitoring client sit outside, and the green band is the modernisation work that moved the system off Laravel 6 and Oracle.

name: Automated Data Pipeline for Executive Power BI Dashboard
description: Containerized Airflow and Spark pipeline that extracts operational data, transforms metrics, loads a PostgreSQL data mart, and feeds executive Power BI dashboards.

screenshots.alt: Sanitized executive energy performance dashboard showing operational, risk, KPI, and financial metrics

problem: Executive performance reporting depended on manual data preparation across multiple operational source systems. This made dashboard refreshes slower, harder to rerun safely, and less consistent across reporting periods.
solution: Built a containerized data pipeline for operational performance dashboards using Apache Airflow, Apache Spark, Docker, PostgreSQL, and MSSQL. The workflow automates extraction from multiple source systems, transforms operational metrics, validates and aggregates business logic, and loads dashboard-ready datasets into a centralized PostgreSQL data mart for Power BI.
proof: Designed the pipeline architecture, Airflow DAG scheduling, Spark ETL logic, SQL transformations, data validation, and rerun-safe refresh flow.
Pipeline supports scheduled refreshes, monthly updates, metric backfill handling, and centralized dashboard-ready tables.
Sanitized dashboard output shows executive-style performance views across operations, asset integrity, safety, risk, KPI, and financial metrics.
result: Reduced manual data preparation and improved the reliability, freshness, and consistency of dashboard reporting, giving executives a cleaner view of performance across reporting periods.

architecture.alt: Data pipeline architecture: three operational databases feed Spark ETL jobs scheduled by Airflow twice a day, loading a PostgreSQL data mart of 13 metrics that Power BI reads
architecture.caption: Airflow schedules two runs a day. Spark extracts from three operational databases, transforms and validates 13 metrics across seven domains, and loads a PostgreSQL data mart with month snapshots, so any run can be repeated or backfilled safely. Power BI reads only the mart.

name: LNG Corporate Website Platform

screenshots.alt: Nusantara Regas corporate website homepage hero showing FSRU infrastructure
Nusantara Regas homepage showing news, company profile, and business chain sections
Nusantara Regas business fields page showing LNG facilities and supply chain content

name: CSIRT Nusantara Regas Public Website
description: Public website of the company's Computer Security Incident Response Team: incident reporting guidance, RFC 2350 documents, PGP public key and the BSSN guide library, built as a hardened static Angular 22 site with no backend to attack.

screenshots.alt: CSIRT Nusantara Regas home page hero with the report-incident call to action and the list of reportable incident types
Live cyber threat map embedded on the home page inside a browser-styled frame
Guide library page with the BSSN incident-handling documents
Contact page with the official channels and the office location map

problem: A CSIRT needs a public, trustworthy front door: how to report an incident, which channels are official, the team's RFC 2350 description and its PGP key. For a security team the site itself must not become an attack surface: no forms to abuse, no server-side code to exploit, and headers that hold up under scrutiny.
solution: I built the site as a static Angular 22 single-page application with standalone components, signals and lazy routes, served by an unprivileged nginx container. Incident reports go by email, optionally PGP-encrypted, so there is no backend and nothing is stored. The production stack adds an edge nginx with TLS, HSTS, request and connection rate limits, GET and HEAD only, a read-only root filesystem, dropped capabilities and an internal network between edge and app. Content lives in typed configuration files: services, reporting steps, incident types, the guide library and the organisation's contact details.
proof: Angular 22 zoneless application with OnPush components, signal inputs and native control flow; production builds enforce bundle budgets of 500 kB warning and 1 MB error.
CSP and security headers included from every nginx location, SPA fallback, gzip, cache rules and a health endpoint; the app container runs nginx-unprivileged on Alpine.
Production Compose with an edge proxy: TLS and HSTS, limit_req and limit_conn per address, only GET and HEAD forwarded, read-only rootfs and cap_drop ALL on both containers.
Accessibility built in: skip link, aria attributes on navigation, visible focus styles, aria-current on active links, and a responsive menu that turns child links into a dropdown or an accordion.
Legacy routes redirect to their new homes, every page sets its own title, and the embedded live threat map falls back to a link-out when the provider blocks framing.
result: The CSIRT has a single public reference for reporting and verification that can be audited line by line: a static bundle, two nginx configurations and no runtime secrets. It is deployed at csirt.nusantararegas.com ahead of its public announcement.

architecture.alt: CSIRT website architecture: incident reporters, constituency staff and peer CSIRTs reach a rate-limited TLS edge nginx, which proxies to an unprivileged nginx serving the static Angular 22 SPA with CSP headers; reports leave by email, and the threat map and static documents sit outside the site
architecture.caption: Visitors hit a rate-limited edge nginx that terminates TLS and forwards only GET and HEAD to an unprivileged nginx serving the static Angular bundle with CSP headers. There is no backend: incident reports travel by email, the threat map is embedded from its provider, and the documents are static assets copied at build time.
